       rogrammable gene-editing technology based on clustered
       regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)–CRISPR-associated
       protein 9 (Cas9)1 has matured into therapeutic approaches that are improving
the lives of patients with various diseases, such as sickle cell disease, β-thalassemia,
and hereditary angioedema.2-4 Precise, corrective CRISPR-Cas9 technology — name-
ly, base editing (which can effect cytosine-to-thymine changes [cytosine base edit-
ing5] or adenine-to-guanine changes [adenine base editing6]) and prime editing7
(which can produce any single-nucleotide change or small insertion or deletion) —
can potentially address more than 90% of pathogenic variants in genetic diseases
that, although rare individually, collectively affect hundreds of millions of people
worldwide.8 However, drug-development efforts have largely focused on recurrent
variants in a few relatively common genetic diseases on account of the extensive
resources needed to develop and bring to market any given therapy.9
    We developed a workflow for the rapid development of customized, corrective
gene-editing therapies for patients with ultrarare or unique “N-of-1” variants
(Fig. 1). More specifically, we developed a base-editing therapy, delivered in vivo to
hepatocytes through lipid nanoparticles, for a single patient who at birth received
a diagnosis of neonatal-onset carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1) deficiency,

INTRODUCTION

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency (CPS1 deficiency) is a urea cycle disorder (UCD)
characterized by life-threatening episodes of hyperammonemia starting in the neonatal period. Despite
standard-of-care therapy with ammonia scavenger medications and dietary therapy, patients experience
recurrent episodes with any minor physiologic stressors1.

Each hyperammonemic episode is associated with a high risk of permanent neurologic damage and death.
It is estimated that 50% of infants with neonatal-onset UCDs die in early infancy2. CPS1 deficiency is an
ultra-rare disease with an estimated incidence of 1:1,300,0003.

Current standard of care for CPS1 deficiency

Humans ingest protein to support growth and the synthesis of a number of key macromolecules. Nitrogen
waste generated from protein catabolism is converted to ammonia, which under normal physiologic
conditions is converted to urea via the urea cycle. Urea can then be excreted in the urine to maintain whole-
body nitrogen homeostasis.

Patients with CPS1 deficiency have impaired activity of the first, rate-limiting step of the urea cycle4
(Figure 1). As such, they experience frequent episodes of neurotoxic hyperammonemia, which can induce
cerebral edema and death. Unfortunately, even when treated with the standard of care, most patients have
recurrent episodes of severe metabolic decompensations and neurologic injury5. It has been noted that
among CPS1 patients that survive the neonatal period, more than 80% go on to have recurrent
hyperammonemia before their first birthday6. Consistent with this data, the CPS1 patient proposed to be
treated with LNP.CPS1.Q335X has had multiple episodes of hyperammonemia during the first five
months of life. Given this high risk of metabolic decompensation, there is a large unmet need for new
effective therapies for CPS1 deficiency, including a clear such need in the present case.

The standard of care focuses on limiting protein intake and catabolism through dietary measures and on
reducing ammonia levels through ammonia scavenger medications (Table 1). Given that these measures
are not very effective, liver transplantation has become the standard of care for severely affected patients
at many institutions7-9. As the urea cycle occurs entirely within the liver, transplantation can normalize
the metabolic defect. However, transplantation is often delayed by donor availability and the need for
neonates to grow to an appropriate size for transplant10. Patients often are not large enough to be transplant
candidates until after their first birthday. During this first year of life, most patients experience irreversible
neurologic damage, even with close medical management5. Liver transplantation is also associated with
acute and chronic risks and challenges.

DRUG SUBSTANCES AND DRUG PRODUCT
Guide RNA drug substance
The guide RNA (gRNA) drug substance in the lipid nanoparticle (LNP) drug product comprised
(1) a 20-nucleotide spacer sequence that corresponded to a protospacer DNA sequence
matching the region of the CPS1 gene spanning the Q335X variant, which included the target
adenosine nucleotide to be corrected by the drug product, and (2) an 80-nucleotide tracrRNA
domain that complexed with a Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) nickase domain in an
adenine base editor (ABE) (Table S1). The gRNA drug substance (originally known as CPS1-
001, then renamed kayjayguran) was a 100-mer oligonucleotide comprising 53 ribonucleotides,
47 2′-O-methylribonucleotides, and 6 phosphorothioate backbone modifications at select
positions, manufactured by IDT using proprietary methods.

Messenger RNA drug substance
The messenger RNA (mRNA) drug substance in the LNP drug product encoded the adenine
base editor 8e (ABE8e) protein with a V106W variant in the adenosine deaminase domain and
with a version of the SpCas9 D10A nickase with a preference for the protospacer-adjacent motif
(PAM) NGC (known as NGC-ABE8e-V106W) (Fig. S1, Table S2). The mRNA drug substance
(known as abengcemeran) comprised the 5′ cap, the 5′ untranslated region (UTR), the ABE
coding sequence, the 3′ UTR, and the 3′ polyadenylate tail; it was manufactured by Aldevron
using proprietary methods. The ABE coding sequence, 4818 nucleotides in length, was codon-
optimized with uridine minimization and had substitution of all uridines with the modified
nucleotide N1-methylpseudouridine.

Lipid nanoparticle drug product
The LNP used was previously described,1 and the specific drug product (originally known as
LNP.CPS1.Q335X, then renamed kayjayguran abengcemeran, or k-abe) was manufactured
under cGMP using processes described in Patent Application WO/2020/061426A2 with the lipid
components (Acuitas Therapeutics® proprietary ionizable cationic lipid ALC-0307 and PEG-lipid
ALC-0159, 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine, and cholesterol) being rapidly mixed
with an aqueous buffer solution containing gRNA and mRNA in a 1:1 ratio by weight, followed
by buffer exchange, sterile filtration, and filling to glass vials for storage until administration.
Ionizable cationic lipid and LNP compositions are described in Patent Applications
WO/2017/004143A1 and WO/2021/030701A1. The clinical batch of the drug product had an
average hydrodynamic diameter of 73 nm with a polydispersity index of 0.07 as determined by
dynamic light scattering, 97% total mRNA encapsulation by the RiboGreen fluorescence assay,
and a gRNA/mRNA ratio of 1.1 as measured by ultra-performance liquid chromatography
(UPLC)-based determinations.

CELLULAR STUDIES

Proof-of-concept studies in cells
To identify a base editing solution for the CPS1 Q335X variant as quickly as possible following
the genetic diagnosis of the patient, we wished to use hepatocytes with the variant. We deemed
it unethical to obtain primary hepatocytes from the patient, and other primary cell types (e.g.,
fibroblasts) were considered inadequate. We instead used the cultured human HuH-7 hepatoma
cell line (Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources Cell Bank) as a proxy for human
hepatocytes. We used a lentiviral vector to transduce human HuH-7 cells with a ≈100-bp CPS1

genomic sequence spanning the Q335X variant, a ≈100-bp CPS1 genomic sequence spanning
the E714X variant (the patient’s second variant), a ≈100-bp PAH genomic sequence spanning
the P281L variant, and a ≈100-bp PAH genomic sequence spanning the R408W variant as
shown in Fig. S2A. The PAH P281L and R408W variant sequences, which are pathogenic
variants for phenylketonuria (PKU), serve as reference controls due to their having validated
base editing solutions that we have previously shown to be efficacious in correcting each variant
in vitro in HuH-7 cells and in vivo in humanized mouse models of PKU.2,3 For this study, we
solely used the PAH P281L variant sequence as a reference control, with ABE8.8 and a P281L-
specific gRNA (designated PAH1) being the optimized base editing solution.2 (For this study,
ultimately neither the CPS1 E714X variant sequence nor the PAH R408W variant sequence
was used.)
We also attempted to use prime editing to introduce the Q335X variant into the endogenous
CPS1 locus in HuH-7 cells, so as not to have to rely solely on the Q335X lentivirus-transduced
HuH-7 cell line for cellular studies. Several attempts were unsuccessful. Accordingly, all cellular
corrective editing data were generated using the Q335X lentivirus-transduced HuH-7 cell line.
As shown in Figs. S2B–2D, using the Q335X lentivirus-transduced HuH-7 cells, we screened a
variety of ABEs in combination with individual candidate gRNAs in plasmid transfection
experiments. Seven gRNAs (designated gRNA3 through gRNA9) tiling the site of the Q335X
variant, such that the variant adenine base ranged from positions 3 through 9 of the protospacer
sequence (Fig. S3) that spanned the ABE editing window, were tested with ABEs compatible
with the PAMs associated with each of the protospacer sequences: SpG for NGN PAMs, SpRY
for all other PAMs (i.e., “near-PAMless”).4 ABEs with three different deaminase domains were
tested: ABE8.8, with the narrowest editing window, ABE8.20, with an intermediate editing
window, and ABE8e, with the broadest window.5,6 In the initial screen (Fig. S2B), the SpG-
ABE8e/gRNA8 combination had the highest corrective editing efficiency for the Q335X variant.
In a secondary transfection screen, we assessed three engineered ABEs with a preference for
NGC PAMs (the extended PAM sequence for gRNA8 is AGCC), designated A1, A2, and A3
(Fig. S2C). The A1 enzyme encodes SpCas9-LWKYQS, differing from wild-type SpCas9 with
the amino acid substitutions D1135L/S1136W/G1218K/E1219Y/R1335Q/T1337S.7 A2 encodes
SpCas9-MQKSER+ with L1111R/D1135M/S1136Q/G1218K/E1219S/R1335E/T1337R, and A3
encodes eSpGC with L1111R/D1135L/S1136W/G1218K/E1219F/A1285K/R1335E/T1337G
(described in Patent Applications WO/2019/040650A1 and WO/2021/151085A2). All versions of
the ABE8e editor with gRNA8 displayed highly efficient corrective editing. In the same
transfection experiment, the well-established solution for the PAH P281L variant (ABE8.8 with
the P281L-specific gRNA, designated PAH1) had similar or less corrective editing efficiency for
the P281L variant (Fig. S2C) compared to the ABE8e editors with gRNA8 for the Q335X
variant.
Because ABE8e has been reported to have gRNA-independent off-target RNA and DNA editing,
the ABE8e-V106W variant, which largely eliminates this off-target editing of ABE8e,6 was used
in a final transfection screen. The SpG, A1, A2, and A3 ABE8e editors, without and with the
V106W variant, in combination with gRNA8 were tested (Fig. S2D). Among the V106W-
containing editors, A1-ABE8e-V106W most closely matched the efficiency of the corresponding
editor without the V106W variant, with the other V106W-containing editors showing reduced
efficiency. In the same transfection experiment, the validated solution for the PAH P281L variant
(ABE8.8 with PAH1) had similar corrective editing efficiency for the P281L variant (Fig. S2D,
red horizontal dotted line) compared to the A1-ABE8e-V106W editor with gRNA8 for the Q335X
variant. Accordingly, a version of gRNA8 with stabilizing chemical modifications, designated
kayjayguran, and the A1-ABE8e-V106W editor, designated NGC-ABE8e-V106W (which, when
encoded in mRNA, is called abengcemeran), were chosen for use in the LNP drug product
